newsitem.title: JORDAN: Palestinian-Israeli tension clouds Jordan bourse.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian-Israeli tension clouds Jordan bourse.

text.p: Jordanian stocks fell further on Monday on the political uncertainty in the region sparked by Israeli-Palestinian tensions, dealers said.
The Amman Financial Market 60-share index dropped 0.20 percent to 147.95 points from 148.25 on Saturday.
A total of 367,806 shares changed hands for 555,356 million dinars ($792 million) in selective buying of blue chips.

"The market has fallen in the past few days because of the recent political developments in the region and a delay in economic legislation promised by the government," said broker Abdul-Mutaleb Abu Hijleh.
"But the overall index of the market has not fallen because highly-capitalised shares, like the Arab Bank, are not going down while the rest on the market witnessed a fall."
Banks dominated trade on Monday, followed by industrials and services.
Market leader Arab Bank which had propelled the index in the first half of September remained unchanged at 242 dinars. The Middle East Investment Bank fell .02 dinars to 1.09 dinars.
The private Pearl Investable Index of the 45 best performing shares on the exchange fell 0.40 percent to 81.60 points, still 14.56 percent down from the same time last year.

King Hussein and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew to Washington on Monday to attend a Middle East summit called on by U.S. President Bill Clinton to try to salvage Middle East peace after recent Palestinian-Israeli violence.

But the Egyptian and Palestinian presidents, in revolt against U.S. diplomacy, asked Clinton on Monday to postpone the meeting set for Tuesday in Washington because they want a clear agenda and assurances.
Fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israeli soldiers have been killed in unrest sparked by the opening of a tunnel in Jerusalem near al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third holiest site on Tuesday.

After gradual gains earlier this month that sent the market back above 150 points last week for the first time in four months, shares began to show signs of fatigue in mid-week with stocks moving lower in thin volume.
Brokers fear the market may be running out of steam as institutional investors continue to wait in the sidelines and stocks run into profit-taking after the bourse's recent results-driven rally.

The market, one of the most politically sensitive bourses in the region, was hit this year by the breakdown of Middle East peace talks and the delay in implementing a limited oil-for-food deal with Jordan's biggest trading partner Iraq.
It is working on a wider package of reforms aimed at making the stock exchange, on a downward trend for two years after a 1992-93 bull run, more efficient, and investor-friendly.

A draft law is due to be put before Jordan's parliament soon which would tighten regulations on accountability and transparency both for brokers and listed companies on the Amman Financial Market (AFM).
